result.summary: The Trojans, urged by Aeneas to fight rather than hide behind their walls, clash with the Danaans in a great battle. Philoctetes wounds Paris with Hercules' arrows, and Paris begs Oenone for healing but is refused and dies on Ida. Helen and Hecuba mourn, and Oenone runs to the pyre and burns with him.

scenes.title: Council before the battle
scenes.summary: Polydamas advises defending the walls, but Aeneas urges open battle and the Trojans arm. Zeus stirs both armies, and Paris is doomed to die by Philoctetes.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk death by famine or siege if they hide, or death in open battle.

scenes.title: The battle rages
scenes.summary: Strife drives the armies together and many warriors fall on both sides. Philoctetes, armed with Hercules' arms, rages through the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Warriors risk death in the slaughter.

scenes.title: Paris is wounded
scenes.summary: Philoctetes kills Cleodorus by mistake, then wounds Paris with two arrows. Paris flees, and at night he goes in agony to Oenone.
scenes.stakes: Paris faces death from the poisoned wound unless Oenone heals him.

scenes.title: Oenone refuses Paris
scenes.summary: Paris pleads for healing; Oenone scornfully drives him away to Helen.
scenes.stakes: Paris's life depends on her mercy; Oenone's own death is fated to follow.

scenes.title: Paris dies; Troy mourns
scenes.summary: Hera and the Seasons discuss the coming fall of Troy while Paris dies on Ida. Hecuba, Helen and the Trojan women lament.
scenes.stakes: Helen fears hatred and violent death from both Greeks and Trojans.

scenes.title: Oenone joins Paris on the pyre
scenes.summary: Oenone runs through the night to Paris's pyre and leaps on it. Their ashes are buried with two pillars turned away from each other.
scenes.stakes: Oenone gives up her life from grief.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic, son of Tydeus (Diomedes is not named in this section).
Son of Achilles (Peleus' son) who kills twelve Trojans.

notable_quotes.reason: Aeneas's call to die gloriously for fatherland rather than languish.
Oenone and Paris burn together on the pyre.
Closing image of pillars turned apart, jealousy preserved in marble.

analysis.text: Fate and pride drive the episode: Paris's doom, Oenone's refusal and her own death are all spun by destiny.
Oenone's grief contrasts with Helen's self-pity and the Trojan women's mourning for their own losses.

legacy.text: Oenone's story of the abandoned nymph who dies for Paris was retold by later poets, notably Tennyson in his poem Oenone (1829).

fun_facts.text: The poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a Greek epic poet of the 3rd–4th century AD, continuing Homer's Iliad.

language_notes.text: The Trojans are burning their dead after the earlier fighting; funeral rites were a sacred duty, which explains their haste and fear of attack.
"Cast a hurried earth-mound o'er the slain" means they quickly heaped a rough burial mound instead of completing proper rites.
"Chode" is the archaic past tense of "chide": here Aeneas rebukes Polydamas sharply.
Thebe and Maeonia were regions of Asia Minor allied to Troy, imagined as sources of grain and wine.
The Trojans claim descent from Zeus, whose son Dardanus founded their royal line.
"Rede" means counsel or advice; the "gallant rede" is Aeneas' speech urging battle.
Strife is called the father's sister of Panic and Fear: they are children of Ares (the war-god), and Strife (Eris) is his sister.
Adamant means an unbreakable metal, here used for Strife's invulnerable armour. Blood-besprent means sprinkled with blood.
Weird means fate or destiny, the lot appointed to a person.
Nor reeked of imminent doom means he did not heed approaching death; to reck is to care about.
Henchmen here means attendants or followers of Epeius, not criminals.
Selene, the Moon goddess, loved the sleeping shepherd Endymion, who was granted endless sleep. The milk-white stream is said to mark the spot.
Hercules' arms were bequeathed to Philoctetes, who lit Hercules' funeral pyre; this is why he carries them.
Hermes killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus, set to guard Io, after lulling his eyes to sleep.
Phaethon borrowed his father the Sun's chariot, lost control and scorched the earth; Zeus struck him down into the river Eridanus.
This is Prometheus, son of Iapetus, chained to Caucasus as punishment for giving fire to humans; an eagle ate his liver daily.
"Shaft" and "dart" both mean arrow; "mark" is the target; "smote" means struck.
"Wont to fence from death" means was accustomed to protect; the buckler (small round shield) normally guarded its bearer.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe"; "scion" means descendant or son.
Poeas' son is Philoctetes, who inherited the bow of Hercules.
"The Unseen Land" is the underworld, the realm of the dead.
"Leeches" here means physicians, not the bloodsucking worms.
"Weird" here means fate or destiny, not strangeness.
Oenone, Paris' first wife, whom he abandoned for Helen, had prophesied that only she could heal him.
Birds flying to the left were taken as bad omens.
"Widowed" is used loosely: Paris means he abandoned Oenone, leaving her like a widow, though he was alive.
The Prayers (Litai) are personified in Homer as Zeus' daughters who follow after Ate (Ruin) and punish those who refuse supplication.
Erinnys: a Fury, a goddess of vengeance who punishes wrongs, especially against supplicants and kin.
Tyndarid: daughter of Tyndareus, i.e. Helen. "Erewhile" means formerly.
Helen was said to be a daughter of Zeus, so rumour calls her immortal or semi-divine.
Love's Queen is Aphrodite, who promised Paris Helen and helped him win her.
"Weird" means fate or destiny; "drave" is an old past tense of drove.
Brakes means thickets or rough undergrowth on the slopes of Mount Ida.
Selene is the Moon goddess; the Seasons (Horae) are here made her daughters by the Sun, a variant genealogy.
Foretells later events: Helenus, a Trojan prince, is later captured and reveals how Troy can fall; Tydeus' son is Diomedes, who takes the Palladium with Odysseus.
Hale means to drag or haul by force.
The image is the Palladium, a statue of Pallas fallen from heaven, believed to guard Troy while it remained.
Wont to lisp means was accustomed to speak baby-talk; the Nymphs had nursed Paris as a child.
Oenone was Paris's first wife, a nymph of Ida, whom he abandoned for Helen.
"Eld" means old age; she dreamed of reaching old age together with Paris.
"So she but find her mate" means "provided only that she find her mate."
"The Cyprian Queen" is Aphrodite (Venus), goddess of love, associated with Cyprus.
The Moon-goddess loved the sleeping shepherd Endymion, so she sympathises with Oenone's love.
Alexander is another name for Paris.
"Death-bale" means funeral pyre; "bale" is an old word for a fire.
"Leal" means loyal, faithful.
Evadne threw herself on the pyre of her husband Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, struck down by Zeus's thunderbolt.

context_notes.text: Polydamas is a Trojan elder known for prudent counsel, who often advises caution and is often overruled.
Troy's walls were said to have been built by gods, Poseidon and Apollo, which is why Polydamas calls them the work of Gods.
Aeneas, son of Anchises and the goddess Aphrodite, is a leading Trojan warrior and later hero of Virgil's Aeneid.
Philoctetes was the Greek archer who held the bow of Heracles, fated to be needed to bring down Troy.
Peleides' son is Neoptolemus, son of Achilles (Peleus' son), fighting with his dead father's spear.
Scylaceus' fate is told in advance: after Troy's fall he flees to Lycia and is killed by the women he brought bad news to.
Phoebus is Apollo; his oracle ordered that Scylaceus be honoured as a hero, a common form of cult.
Hephaestus was the smith-god who made divine armour and tools.
Cleodorus is a Greek fighter from Rhodes, the island named as his mother's home.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, used throughout this poem.
Oenone is a Nymph of Mount Ida. Her handmaids attend her.
Paris was shot with a poisoned arrow by Philoctetes; only Oenone, his abandoned first wife, a nymph skilled in healing, could cure him.
Paris' abduction of Helen caused the Trojan War, in which gods' own children, such as Sarpedon, died.
Hera favoured the Greeks and hated Troy, since Paris had judged Aphrodite fairer than her.
Hector, Priam's greatest son, was killed by Achilles; his tomb is where Priam mourns.
Helen is Paris's wife, whose abduction caused the Trojan War.
Oenone, a mountain nymph, was Paris's first wife. He abandoned her for Helen, and she refused to heal his fatal wound.
Paris was raised as a shepherd on Mount Ida, so the shepherds honour him as their former comrade.

literary_notes.text: Aeneas is shown as proud and aggressive, equating withdrawal with cowardice and favoring honorable open combat over caution.
Glorious death in battle is set against a lingering death by famine, sharpening Aeneas' argument for fighting.
The narrator announces Paris' death in advance, casting a fated shadow over the coming battle and echoing the book's opening line.
Strife and Battle become a cloaked goddess stalking the field, with Panic and Fear as her attendants.
A chain of three comparisons (winds, fire, sea) piles up sound imagery to convey the roar of the armies.
The narrator's cry 'Ah fool!' reacts to Galenus' blindness to his fate, heightening irony.
Warriors are likened to wasps killed by a vinegrower, making Aeneas' killing of the looters seem swift and easy.
The soul driven out like a scattering breath makes death seem sudden and weightless.
Philoctetes is compared to the war-god and to a flooding river breaking dykes, showing his unstoppable force.
The remark that Paris's last day met him hints at his coming death at Philoctetes' hands.
The arrow's sudden fall is compared to an ambusher leaping out, stressing how unexpected the death is.
Paris is likened to a dog that attacks a lion and then flees, mocking his courage.
Piled corpses are compared to hail and snowflakes, conveying their number and how thickly they fall.
The seducer who abandoned Oenone must now beg her for his life.
The ill-omened birds and visions of doom hint that Paris will not be saved by Oenone.
Paris' agony is compared to a man parched with thirst and burning with fever, making the pain physical.
Paris begs mercy from the wife he betrayed, and her mocking repetition of "thou" underlines the reversal of their positions.
Oenone's wish to tear flesh and lap blood like a tigress shows the violence of her long-suppressed hatred.
The narrator anticipates Oenone's own death, suggesting her refusal will soon cost her too.
Fate spinning a thread pictures destiny as weaving, with her life's length already fixed.
The goddesses' talk previews Troy's fall: Helenus's capture, the theft of the Palladium, and the ruin that follows.
Hecuba's fears of sacked city and captive women anticipate what will actually happen to Troy.
Helen's lament is revealed as self-centred, showing her guilt and fear rather than true grief for Paris.
The one truly grieving mourner is the wife Paris deserted, not those who loudly lament him.
Her melting into tears is compared to snow thawing into streams, an extended image of grief flowing and dissolving her.
Her wasting away like wax before a flame shows hidden grief consuming her.
A heifer racing heedlessly toward her mate conveys Oenone's blind, instinctive desire to reach Paris.
The Moon-goddess pities Oenone and lights her path, making nature sympathetic to her.
Even in death the pillars keep turning away, so the old jealousy and estrangement outlast the lovers' union in fire.
